You are ADVERSARIALLY VERIFYING one review finding about the repository at
/home/user/adss-2026-09-07, on branch claude/adss-slice-04-revenue-per-order-month.

FINDING: A DAS contract description carries business meaning, restating dab/model.yaml's definition
FILE: /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/das/contracts/order_details.yaml:48
DETAIL: The `unit_price` column's description reads: "Edm.Decimal with Scale=Variable, Nullable=false. The scale is pinned here because the source does not pin it. **This is the price on the line, which is not necessarily the product's current price.**" (lines 46-49).

That last sentence is business meaning, and it is a second copy of a definition that already exists: `dab/model.yaml:149-152` defines `AGREED_UNIT_PRICE` as "The price per unit the business agreed to on this line" with the description "What was agreed when the order was accepted, which is not what the goods cost today and does not move when the price does."

This breaks two hard rules:
- §1.1: "A contract's `description` stays in system vocabulary: the source's type, its nullability, what the source calls it. **Never what it means to the business.**"
- §1.2: "Every entity, attribute and relationship has a `definition` in business language, and that is the **only** place the data is explained."

The file's own header comment (lines 3-4) states the rule it breaks: "Descriptions stay in the source's vocabulary -- what a thing MEANS is dab/model.yaml's job, and saying it twice is how two numbers start disagreeing."

Every other column in this repository's three contracts obeys it — `orders.yaml` and `customers.yaml` carry only Edm types, nullability, referential constraints and spelling notes; `order_details.yaml`'s own `freight`-equivalent line 47 ("The scale is pinned here because the source does not pin it") is fine because it is about the recording. Only this one sentence crosses over. The fix is to delete it; `AGREED_UNIT_PRICE` already says it.
WHY IT MATTERS: This is the exact drift §1.1 and §1.2 exist to prevent: the meaning of the price now lives in two files, and the day the model's definition is refined the contract will be the stale copy nobody regenerates. It is also precedent — the next contract author reads this file as the pattern.

test if that settles it. Look for the reason the finding is wrong: a check elsewhere that
already catches it, a documented decision that accepts it on purpose (docs/adr/,
docs/deviations.md, docs/conventions.md, the question documents), an invariant that makes the
bad input impossible, or a simple misreading.

Do NOT modify any file. If you must experiment, copy to a scratch directory.

recorded as a known limitation. confidence is 0-10: how sure you are, having tried to break
your own conclusion. If isReal, give the smallest correct fix.

# Deviations register

Every knowing departure from a principle in [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) or a hard rule in
[conventions.md](conventions.md) is recorded here, with the ADR that decided it.

The register exists because an unregistered exception is indistinguishable from a mistake. Once
one exists, the next person reads it as precedent and copies it, and a year later the rule is
folklore. Writing the cost down keeps the trade visible; writing an exit condition down keeps it
from becoming permanent by default.

A deviation is legitimate only when all four fields are answerable. If the cost cannot be named,
the deviation has not been understood. If the exit condition cannot be named, it is not a
deviation but a change of rule, and the rule should be superseded instead.

## Entries

| # | Rule deviated from | Why | Cost | Exit condition | ADR | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-0001 | [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) **R2 — No cross-dependency**: "a data product owns its structures and does not consume another product's" | Every slice's page reads one generated Unified Star Schema in `dar__uss`. The structure being shared is additive by construction — keys inherit along many-to-one relationships, measures stay on the stage that owns them — so the fan trap R2 exists to prevent cannot occur **in the measures** — demonstrated in slice 4, the first with two grains: freight is 64,942.69 and revenue 1,265,793.0395 over the whole bridge and per month alike, though 2155 line rows carry an order key. It **can** occur in the peripherals, which is the half this entry asserted too broadly for three slices: a numeric attribute that is also a measure's source is published twice, and `sum(order.freight_charge)` over the bridge returns 207,306.10. ADR 0012 states the rule and refuses a question that breaks it. One shared calendar is what lets two processes be compared at all. Generating a private copy per page would make that comparison a cross-schema join, which is most of what a USS is for | A change made for one reader is visible to all of them the moment it is generated. There is no per-reader projection, so "this reader may not see freight" cannot be expressed. Two readers cannot hold different definitions of the same measure. The first thing to break is a slice needing a measure defined one way for one reader and another way for another — it will have to be modelled as two measures | A second consumer needs isolation: a different shape of the same structure, or a group that must not see part of it. The generator then gains per-group projections over the same bridge and this entry is resolved | [0002](adr/0002-dar-is-one-generated-unified-star-schema.md) | open |

| D-0002 | [conventions.md](conventions.md) **§1.1 — DAS keeps the source's words and types**: a contract records what the source sent | The contract vocabulary has `DOUBLE` and `DECIMAL` and no `REAL`, so an `Edm.Single` cannot be recorded faithfully — both options are a choice. `DECIMAL` is chosen because a `NaN` or an `Infinity` then fails at the cast, at `das unpack`, rather than propagating into a measure where both of a question's answers would agree on it and the gate would stay green | A source value with more than the declared scale is refused rather than approximated, which is the right failure and still a failure somebody must handle. And the contract no longer says what the source's metadata says, so a reader comparing the two finds a difference the file does not explain — this entry is that explanation | The contract vocabulary gains a type that is a faithful transcription of a 32-bit float, or the source stops sending one | [0011](adr/0011-a-float-in-the-source-is-recorded-as-a-decimal.md) | open |

## Entry format

Entries are appended in the order they are decided and never removed. A resolved deviation is
marked resolved, with the date and the commit or ADR that resolved it, because the history of why
something looked necessary is worth as much as the fact that it no longer is.

Field by field:

* **Rule deviated from** — quote or link the exact rule. "The spirit of layering" is not a rule;
  a row in a blueprint table is.
* **Why** — the constraint that made the conforming option unworkable *here*. Convenience, time
  pressure and unfamiliarity are not constraints; they are reasons to do it properly.
* **Cost** — what this buys the system in trouble. Name the first thing that will break, who pays
  for it, and which future change it makes more expensive. A deviation with no cost is evidence
  the rule is wrong, so supersede the rule instead of deviating from it.
* **Exit condition** — the observable thing that has to become true for the deviation to be
  removed. "When we have time" is not observable.
* **ADR** — the decision record that argued it. Every deviation has one; the register is the
  index, the ADR is the argument.
* **Status** — `open` while it stands, `resolved` once it is gone.

## Review

The register is read at the start of every slice. Each open entry is checked against its exit
condition **and against whether its argument is still being carried on assertion**. D-0001 is
what that clause was written for. Its justification rests on measures not multiplying across a
walk over many-to-one edges; slice 2 built the first edge but both its entities were at one
grain, so the walk was exercised and the property was not. Slice 4 brought the second grain and
measured it, which is where the argument stopped being carried on assertion — and the same
measurement found that the argument was half wrong, which three slices of re-reading the entry
had not. That is the clause earning its place: an entry can be true, unexamined, and misleading
all at once. An entry should also be re-read the moment a second consumer appears, not only
when isolation is demanded, because by then the shared structure will already have shaped both
readers. An entry whose exit condition has been met and which is still open is a defect in the
same way a failing test is: the system is no longer doing what its own documentation says.

### 1.1 DAS — the source-vocabulary exemption

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| DAS object and column names mirror the source. The source's own words are **required** here, even where other layers forbid them. | DAS exists to say what the source said. Renaming a source field to a business term buries an interpretation in the layer that must make none. | Hard rule |
| The mechanical translation is expected: a source property becomes `snake_case`, a source entity set becomes a `snake_case` plural table named after the source's own word for it. | A consistent spelling of the source's word is still the source's word. | Hard rule |
| A contract file's stem is the landed table name, and that name is used in every schema of this layer. | One name for one thing, so grepping for a table finds its contract. | Hard rule |
| A source name that would be a violation anywhere else — `ShipVia`, `total_orders` — is **not** a violation here. | It is a column in a table nobody on this side controls. A rule that cannot tell that case from a name we chose produces false accusations. | Hard rule |
| A contract's `description` stays in system vocabulary: the source's type, its nullability, what the source calls it. Never what it means to the business. | Business meaning has exactly one home (§1.2). | Hard rule |
| Columns this layer adds itself carry no source's word and are named for what they record: `payload`, `source_system`, `source_entity`, `source_url`, `extracted_at`, `extracted_on`. | Provenance is ours, not the source's, and must be tellable apart from it at a glance. | Hard rule |
| A landed record is **one whole source record from one response**. Composing a landed row from more than one response is forbidden. | Blueprint S4 requires provenance per *data point*. One record per row makes a field's provenance the record's provenance — which is true only while that holds, and silently false the moment a row is composed from two responses. | Hard rule |
| **No loader vocabulary crosses into `das__staged`.** `_dlt_load_id` and `_dlt_id` stay in `das__raw`; the staged view exposes `extracted_at` and `extracted_on`, derived from the load id, and nothing else of the loader's. | The blueprint's first promise is that every tool is replaceable without invalidating a principle. A loader's column name in the layer's published interface welds that loader in, in the layer everything else is rebuilt from. The derivation is injective, so no provenance is lost. | Hard rule |
| A contract generates two staged objects: `das__staged.<table>`, the change log with one row per source record per load, and `das__staged.<table>__current`, one row per key from the latest load that carried it. | DAS is append-only (S2), so the change log is what it actually holds and is what DAB historizes from. `__current` exists because a question asked of the source needs one row per thing, not one per observation. | Hard rule |

### 1.2 DAB — the business vocabulary

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| Entity and attribute identifiers are `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`, with `id` and `name` holding the identical string. A **relationship** carries only a `name` — the modelling grammar has no `id` field for one — and its identifier is composed, `<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, per M6. | It is the modelling language's convention, and the visual break from every other layer's lower case makes a leak obvious on sight. | Hard rule |
| Entity and attribute names are **singular**: `ORDER`, `ORDER_LINE`, `SHIP_COUNTRY`. | An entity names a kind of thing, not a pile of them. The pile is what a query produces. | Hard rule |
| Descriptive attributes are prefixed with their entity (`CUSTOMER_NAME`, `ORDER_LINE_ID`); generic ones and measures are not (`STATUS`, `QUANTITY`). | The prefix is what makes an attribute readable once it has been inherited into a wide DAR row. | Guideline |
| **No source name appears anywhere in `dab/model.yaml`** — not in an id, not in a name, not in a definition, not in a description. | This is the layer whose purpose is source-agnosticism; a source name in it means the dependency was moved rather than broken. | Hard rule |
| Source names may appear in `dab/mappings/**`, and only in `table`, `primary_keys` and `transformation_expression`. | A mapping's entire job is to bind two vocabularies, and it cannot do that without naming both. Confining them to three keys is what keeps the binding auditable. | Hard rule |
| `dab/uss.yaml` is governed by §1.3 and §2, not by this section. | It lives beside the model but it declares DAR things. One directory, two regimes; this sentence is the arbiter. | Hard rule |
| Every entity, attribute and relationship has a `definition` in business language, and that is the **only** place the data is explained. | Everything else — contracts, questions, the generated layer, the app — references these. Two definitions eventually mean two numbers. | Hard rule |
| A relationship name is a verb phrase, so `<SOURCE>_<NAME>_<TARGET>` reads as a sentence: `ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER`. | Direction is the thing people get wrong, and a sentence cannot be read backwards by accident. | Hard rule |
| Names say what a thing *is* to the business, not how it is stored or derived: `PLACED_ON`, not `ORDER_DATE_TS`. | The physical shape changes; the concept does not. | Guideline |
| Prefer the word the business already uses over a more precise one it does not. | A model nobody recognises is a model nobody checks. | Guideline |

### 1.3 DAR — the generated layer

Names here are emitted by the generator, so these rules are what the generator implements. They
are on this page because they are the contract every consumer is written against.

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| Object names are `snake_case` **singular**, derived from the entity: `order`, `order_line`. A reserved word is quoted (`dar__uss."order"`), never abbreviated around. | Same reason as §1.2, in the other layer's spelling. | Structural columns carry a leading underscore: `_bridge`, `_calendar`, `_stage`, `_event`, `_event_date`, `_is_current`, `_measure__…`. | The underscore says "the generator owns this". Anything without one came from the business model. | Hard rule |
| The calendar's own columns are the exception, and carry none: `date_key`, `year_number`, `month_label`. | It is the one object the generator invents whole rather than deriving from the model, so there is no business name for its columns to be confused with, and these are the names a reader of any star schema already knows. | Hard rule |
| Measure columns are `_measure__<entity>__<measure>`, where `<measure>` is the **whole** §2 name. `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`, not `_measure__order__placed`. | §2's payoff is searchability by any of the three parts, and that only holds if the whole name survives into the physical column. It costs long, repetitive column names; that is the price of the name being the same everywhere. | Hard rule |
| The generator **never invents a member**. A null dimension stays null; there is no "Unknown" row, no "N/A" country, no placeholder date. | An invented member is meaning with no definition behind it, and §1.2 says meaning has exactly one home. A question that wants nulls grouped or excluded says so in the question file, where the choice belongs. | Hard rule |
| The generator names every column it reads from a DAB view. It never selects `*` from `dab.*`. | daana's presentation views are themselves `SELECT *` over table macros, so a model change silently changes their shape. Naming the columns turns that into a regeneration diff. | Hard rule |
| **Nothing in this layer is hand-edited.** A wrong name is fixed in the business model and regenerated. | Blueprint R4. An edit to generated output is lost on the next generation. | Hard rule |

### 1.4 DAB — mapping rules

A mapping says how one entity is loaded from DAS. These rules exist because daana accepts several
kinds of wrong mapping without complaint, and two of them corrupt data silently.

| # | Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | `table:` names a `das__staged` object and nothing else. Never a subquery, never a join, never `das__raw`. | Blueprint F3. A join here is business logic in the wrong layer; a raw read skips the contract's casts and the contract stops being the gate. | Hard rule |
| M2 | Exactly **one** `primary_keys` entry, whose VARCHAR result is the entity key: a bare string column, `cast(col AS VARCHAR)`, or casts joined with `||` and a separator. Never `concat` for a composite key. | Two entries are two *alternate identifiers* to daana, not a composite key: the engine refuses them at deploy unless `allow_multiple_identifiers` is set on the mapping group, and with it set the entity key becomes a **minted UUID** with nothing in DAS to recompute it from — so the layer stops being rebuildable from its source. `||` yields null when a part is null; `concat` ignores nulls and `concat_ws` drops the separator too, so either turns a missing half into a shorter key that collides with a real one. A join without a separator makes `'A1' + '23'` and `'A12' + '3'` the same key, and a separator that can occur in a part does not fix it. ADR 0010. | Hard rule |
| M3 | `ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG`. `FULL` is permitted only against a source view **proven** to hold exactly one row per key, and the proof is a data check, not a claim. | Observed: `FULL` against a multi-row-per-key source inserts one duplicate `_desc` row per execute, forever, and every presentation view hides it. Our staged change log is multi-row-per-key by construction, so `FULL` is the wrong default here and the failure is invisible. | Hard rule |
| M4 | `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at`. | Blueprint B3. The effective time of a fact is when DAS observed it. Anything else dates the fact by something that is not about the fact — and no source here reports when it changed. | Hard rule |
| M5 | An attribute expression reads its own row: a column, a cast, or **arithmetic over columns of that row** — including a same-row function such as `date_diff`. Never a subquery, never an aggregate, never a reach into another table. | An expression that reaches beyond the row is a join, and every join must come from a declared relationship. Arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies, so it needs no definition of its own beyond the attribute it lands in. | Hard rule |
| M5a | What arithmetic does **not** cover: a `CASE`, a default, a coalesce that invents one, a filter, a bucket, or anything that changes the grain. Those go in the model as an attribute with a definition. | Each of them is a choice somebody made, and a choice needs a definition beside it. Every `CASE` is over columns *and* on their values, so listing it as permitted above and forbidden here decided nothing; by this rule's own test a `CASE` is always a choice. The mechanical check cannot tell arithmetic from a bucket — it is four keywords and seven function names — so this line is the rule and the regex is only its cheapest half. ADR 0007. | Hard rule |
| M6 | A relationship's `id` is `<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`; its `source_table` is byte-identical to a `table` in its mapping; its target expression has the same **shape** as the target entity's own key expression — the same casts and the same functions, though the column may be named differently. Every edge the model declares is loaded by some mapping, and every edge a mapping loads is declared by the model. | A mismatched `source_table` is skipped silently, and a key of a different shape produces pairs that join to nothing. Neither says anything at load time. The shape is what matters and the spelling is not: a foreign key is routinely named differently from the primary key it points at, and it is the casting and the functions that decide the VARCHAR the two sides produce. | Hard rule |
| M7 | Every mapped table carries at least one attribute. | daana refuses to deploy an entity with none, and the failure arrives at deploy rather than at review. | Hard rule |

content.content:
One contract per source entity set. **The file stem is the landed table name** and is the
name used in every DAS schema, so grepping for a table finds its contract.

## Adding a source

1. Write `das/contracts/<table>.yaml`. Copy an existing one; the keys are fixed.
2. `uv run adss das record --contract <table>` — hits the live service, writes fixtures.
   Read the diff: it is what the source actually sends.
3. `uv run adss das ingest && uv run adss das unpack`.
4. The generated checks under `checks/` are committed; the view SQL under `das/sql/` is
   not, because it embeds the lake's absolute path. `adss das unpack --check` fails if the
   committed checks are not what the contracts generate.

## What the contract may and may not say

`description` stays in the source's vocabulary: its type, its nullability, what the source
calls it. **Never what it means to the business** — that has exactly one home, and it is not
here.

The format cannot express business logic. There is no key for an expression, a filter, a
default or a coalesce, and one that looks like it is refused when the contract is read. If
you need one, you are in the wrong layer.

`target_name` must be the mechanical `snake_case` of `source_path`. Not a rename. A rename
buries an interpretation in the layer that is supposed to make none.

## Things that cost a day if you do not know them

- **`union_by_name => true` is not optional.** Without it, a column that appears only in a
  later load is silently dropped from the glob. No error. Just missing data.
- **`hive_types` is not optional either**, or the partition key comes back as text.
- **`DECIMAL` takes `precision` and `scale` as their own keys.** YAML splits a flow mapping
  on the comma inside `DECIMAL(18, 4)`, so the contract silently becomes `DECIMAL(18`.
- **The loader does not stop inferring when told to limit nesting.** Top-level keys are
  still split into typed columns, and it will make a decimal into a floating-point number.
  The payload column hint is what stops it.
- **`das__raw` becomes `das_raw`** unless dataset-name normalisation is disabled. A warning
  is all you get.
- **Paths in views are absolute.** A relative one resolves at query time, so a view created
  from the repository root breaks when a page opens the same warehouse from elsewhere.

feat(dar): let a stage inherit its date, and record the lines that need one

The generator half of ADR 0009. date_attribute may now name <ENTITY>.<ATTRIBUTE>, and the date
is resolved in the same CTE and at the same instant as the key -- off the same parent row the
walk had already found. An unqualified name still means the event's own entity, which is every
event declared so far.

What the record promised and the first draft did not do: a row whose inherited date does not
resolve gets no bridge row. The version CTE filters its own date, and an inherited one is not
there to filter, so the stage filters where it was resolved. Without it the row would reach the
bridge dated null and the calendar's inner join would drop it -- which looks exactly like the
rule working, and is not.

Four mutations are caught, and two of them only after the tests were sharpened. Asserting that
the date appears in the right CTE said nothing about where the STAGE reads it from, so taking
it from the event's own entity stayed green; and asserting the parent's column said nothing
about the as-of predicate, so an unbounded join to the parent's history stayed green too. Both
now fail. A date on an entity no edge reaches is refused by name, with the edges that do exist
listed, rather than by the bare KeyError that used to come out of the model.

Also records the order lines: 2155 of them, 2155 distinct composite keys, and a discount
recorded as a decimal rather than a double per ADR 0011 -- so a NaN fails at the cast instead
of becoming a month's revenue that both answers agree on.
